questions.question: Apply exportation: rewrite (p∧q)→r as an equivalent nested implication with no conjunction left of the arrow.
questions.explanation: Exportation states (p∧q)→r ≡ p→(q→r): a conjunction in the antecedent can be split into two nested conditionals.

questions.question: Let p = 'the test passes' and q = 'every case ran'. Express 'the test passes if and only if every case ran' without using ↔, as a conjunction of two implications.
questions.explanation: Material equivalence: p↔q ≡ (p→q)∧(q→p) — a biconditional is a conjunction of the implication and its converse.

questions.question: Apply transposition to (p∧q)→r so that the negated consequent becomes the antecedent. What is the resulting implication?
alternatives: not r implies not (p and q)
questions.explanation: Transposition replaces an implication by its contrapositive: (p∧q)→r ≡ ¬r→¬(p∧q), equivalently ¬r→(¬p∨¬q) by De Morgan.

questions.question: What simplifies (p∧q)∨(p∧¬q)?
questions.explanation: Factor out p by distributivity.

questions.question: Write 'exactly one of p and q is true' as a two-disjunct formula using only ∧, ∨, ¬ — a DNF capturing XOR.
alternatives: (p and not q) or (not p and q)
questions.explanation: XOR holds when p is true and q false, or vice versa: (p∧¬q)∨(¬p∧q), equivalently (p∨q)∧¬(p∧q).

questions.question: Eliminate the implication from ¬p→q using p→q ≡ ¬p∨q, then simplify. Which disjunction results?
questions.explanation: ¬p→q rewrites to ¬¬p∨q, and double negation elimination leaves p∨q.

questions.question: Simplify (p∧q)∨(¬p∧r)∨(q∧r) by identifying the term already covered whenever one of the other two holds. Which single conjunct is redundant?
questions.explanation: By the consensus theorem (p∧q)∨(¬p∧r)∨(q∧r) ≡ (p∧q)∨(¬p∧r): if q∧r is true, then p makes the first term true or ¬p makes the second true, so q∧r adds no new satisfying rows.

questions.question: Having verified p∨True ≡ True in a truth table, a student concludes p∧False ≡ False without any further work. Which principle — swap ∧↔∨ and True↔False — legitimizes the shortcut?
questions.explanation: The duality principle says interchanging ∧ with ∨ and the constants True/False turns any valid Boolean identity into another valid identity.

questions.question: What simplifies (p→q)∧(p→¬q)?
questions.explanation: Both implications require p false.

questions.question: A simplifier replaces the subformula p→q inside (p→q)∧r with ¬p∨q, yielding (¬p∨q)∧r, on the ground that equivalent subformulas can be swapped while preserving the whole formula's truth value. Which theorem licenses this move?
questions.explanation: The replacement (substitution) theorem: if φ ≡ ψ, then replacing an occurrence of φ by ψ in any formula yields an equivalent formula.

questions.question: How is ((p∨q)∧(¬p∨r))→(q∨r) classified?
questions.explanation: This is the resolution principle: q∨r follows from the two clauses, making the implication always true.

questions.question: What is the dual of the formula p∧(q∨False)?
questions.explanation: Duality swaps ∧ with ∨ and False with True.

questions.question: Express p⊕q in terms of the biconditional.
questions.explanation: XOR is true exactly when the operands differ — the negation of the biconditional.

questions.question: What is (p→q)∨(p→r) equivalent to?
What is (p→r)∧(q→r) equivalent to?
Simplify step by step: ¬(¬p∧q) ∧ (p∨q).
questions.explanation: De Morgan gives (p∨¬q)∧(p∨q); distribution yields p∨(¬q∧q) = p∨False = p.

questions.question: Classify (p→q)∨(q→p): tautology, contradiction, or contingency?
questions.explanation: If q is true, q→p holds; if q is false, p→q holds. Every row is covered, so the disjunction is always true.

questions.question: Evaluate all four rows of (p↔q)↔p and express the result as a formula in q alone.
questions.explanation: Rows TT, TF, FT, FF give T, F, T, F — the column of q itself, so (p↔q)↔p ≡ q.

questions.question: Using p→x ≡ ¬p∨x twice and then distributing, rewrite (p→q)∧(p→r) as a single implication.
questions.explanation: (¬p∨q)∧(¬p∨r) factors to ¬p∨(q∧r), which is p→(q∧r).

questions.question: Give one truth assignment for which p⊕q is true while p↔q is false.
questions.explanation: XOR holds exactly when the operands differ — precisely the rows where the biconditional fails.
